questions.topic: Why a track rather than a point
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a track records more than a single point
questions.stem: A planning memo describes a detector that records a sequence of sensor hits along a particle path. Why does the memo favour a track over a single position measurement?

options.text: A single point cannot show which way the particle moved through the detector
options.misconception: believes a single point already fixes the travel direction

options.text: Tracks use fewer sensors, so the detector can be built more cheaply
options.misconception: assumes tracks are cheaper because they need fewer sensors

options.text: The sequence of hits gives the direction of travel and the path length
Point detectors can only register charged particles, while tracks register all

questions.explanation: An ordered set of hits fixes the direction of travel and the path length. A single point gives only where the particle was, and the memo needs to know it came from above rather than from the side.

options.misconception: misreads the ratio of ten thousand as a factor of ten

options.text: Most muons pass through the rock without being detected at all

The rock absorbs every muon that reaches 3000 m of overburden
options.misconception: believes the overburden stops every incoming muon

questions.explanation: A background one ten-thousandth of the surface value is far easier to tell apart from a rare signal. That is why detectors go underground, since fewer muons imitate the events sought.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: The two laws constraining a spectrum
questions.learningObjective: Identify the two laws that fix the shape and total of a thermal spectrum
questions.stem: A memo reports that a body of material glows across the whole spectrum with a single temperature. Explain the two laws that fix both the shape of that spectrum and the total power it emits.

answer.exemplar: The shape is fixed by Planck's law, which gives the energy per unit frequency for a radiator at a given temperature, and the total is fixed by the Stefan-Boltzmann law, which says the power per unit area scales with the fourth power of the temperature. Together they mean a hotter body emits more at every wavelength and peaks at a shorter wavelength.

questions.explanation: Planck law sets the shape of the spectrum at a given temperature, while the Stefan-Boltzmann law sets the total power per area. The temperature fixes both colour and brightness.
questions.hint: One law for shape, one for total power.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What the background temperature indicates
questions.learningObjective: Apply Wien's law to a background temperature
questions.stem: A memo table lists the relic background radiation at 2.725 K. Using Wien's displacement law with a constant of 2.898 times ten to the minus three metre kelvin, what peak wavelength in millimetres does that imply?
questions.explanation: Wien's law gives the peak wavelength as the constant divided by the temperature, so 2.898e-3 over 2.725 is about 1.06e-3 m, which is 1.06 mm. Today's microwave receivers see exactly that band.
questions.hint: Divide the constant by the temperature.

answer.exemplar: A larger redshift corresponds to a larger recession speed and therefore a greater distance, so the galaxy at 0.10 lies far beyond the one at 0.01. answer.exemplar: Expansion stretches every photon wavelength, and because photon energy falls as the wavelength grows, each photon carries less energy and the radiation appears colder.
